codes.reason: Rather than treating the four identification types as outcomes of dream building and positive programming succeeding or failing, the reading explains them as sequential stages along a member's tenure trajectory (pp. 461–463, 477).

The reading reinterprets the passages on encapsulated and ambivalent members as two consecutive moments of the same sequence—yielding to an outsider's skepticism in person and adopting upline framing afterward—rather than evidence of two distinct member states (pp. 475–476, 480–481).

The reading reverses the causal sequence on p. 477 by arguing that former distributors left within their first year before repeated socialization practices had run, so early departure prevented identification rather than failed identification causing departure.

The reading re-examines the second disidentified informant's account on p. 479 to show that his opposition was already set during a coercive recruitment pitch, with no printed evidence of a dream, a failed upline relationship, or outside confidants.

Keeping the outcome that dream building and positive programming together produce positive identification, the reading replaces the sensebreaking-and-sensegiving meaning mechanism with behavioral commitment generated by freely chosen, costly public actions (pp. 469, 474, 476).

The reading reverses the causal order in the account of ambivalent identification by arguing that not distributing comes first and leaves non-member ties intact because an inactive member never approaches friends and family (pp. 474, 480).

Without disputing that reported finances failed to sort distributors, the reading questions the premise on p. 463 that financial performance is an independent measure separable from identification, since whether a member counts training expenses as costs already expresses their stance toward Amway.

The reading inverts the claim that a strong supportive upline bond channels members into organizational activity and encapsulated sensemaking, arguing from pp. 479–480 that the durable sponsor tie with an inactive member holds only because it does not depend on doing the work and brings about none of that conduct.

The reading re-examines the dream-building outing in the Appendix (pp. 492–493) to argue that it scarcely links wanted possessions to the downline's self and instead builds the mentoring bond and models the upline's manner inside the very first session.

The reading keeps seekership among identifying members as the outcome but attributes it to pre-existing discontent with work, finances, or family brought into Amway rather than to sensebreaking unsettling a settled sense of self (pp. 464–467, 470–471).

The reading recapitulates the paper's account on pp. 464–469 of how dream building serves as Amway's primary sensebreaking practice by tying desired possessions to the self, creating identity deficits relative to a comfort zone, and renewing those drives with larger dreams.

The reading keeps encapsulation and its alternatives as outcomes but attributes them to how a distributor's pre-existing circle of family, friends, and coworkers reacts when approached rather than to Amway's positive programming (pp. 472–474, 479–481).

Pointing out that p. 463 only observed gross sales volume while leaving net profit and upward transfers unmeasured, the reading holds that whether net money flows to or from a distributor may sort with the direction of their identification.

The reading questions the premise that sensebreaking is a single unified process, separating stated dissatisfaction with one's present life from excitement about dreams to argue that failed sensebreaking on p. 477 conflates two distinct conditions.

The reading re-examines the passages on pp. 478–479 to show that none of the disidentified informants exhibits both surviving dream-inspired seekership and a failed upline bond, arguing that the passages instead separate opposed from detached leavers by whether they experienced a wrong at the hands of recruiters or upline.

The reading challenges the premise that dream building and positive programming are two separate practices, arguing that dream building occurs inside the mentoring relationship so that the two-by-two model collapses into a single dimension of upline bond quality (pp. 462–466, 477–482).

The reading reinterprets the evidence on p. 463—that distributors could not or would not state net profits, disagreed over counting training materials as expenses, and earned minimal gross income—as showing that identification types reflect whether members have reckoned their financial losses rather than that finances are irrelevant.
